realism_reviews.notes:
COMPARISON SCOPE. Compared against the entire canonical bank at the represented candidate 78a107f402e33a40dc210635822d8a8314359a9b: 294 question records enumerated from data/questions, 293 compared pairwise against MA-Q-0288. No sampling was used and the existing duplicate report was not relied on. Metrics computed for every pair were stem token Jaccard, whole-item token Jaccard over stem plus all choices, best single-choice token Jaccard, shared rule_ids, and shared area, topic, subtopic, question_type and family_id. Additionally compared against the two exact frozen B3-A R1 repaired variants at c7b438f253089b74231e50040603458d46d20e6c, MA-Q-0241 and MA-Q-0256, as supplemental future-production comparators.

STRONGEST COMPARATORS. (1) MA-Q-0289 is the strongest comparator overall. It is the only bank item sharing a rule_id with MA-Q-0288 (MA-PMP-REGISTRATION-DUTY) and the only other item under topic 'Pharmacist practice'; its subtopic is 'Monitoring program registration' against 'Determinations versus adjacent duties'. Textual overlap is nevertheless low: stem Jaccard 0.035, whole-item Jaccard 0.101, best single-choice Jaccard 0.200. The two items are complementary rather than duplicative. MA-Q-0289 is SBA and tests the substance of the 247 CMR 9.15(1) duty, namely that registration and login maintenance are personal to the dispensing pharmacist and not discharged by the pharmacy's institutional MassPAT account. MA-Q-0288 is SATA and tests the enumerated determination set in 247 CMR 9.15(2), where the monitoring programme appears only as a rejected proposition. A candidate can miss one and answer the other correctly, and the discriminations tested do not overlap. The stems share a stylistic opening ('A newly licensed' against 'A newly hired' Massachusetts pharmacist), noted here for completeness; it is an authoring cadence common to entry-of-practice vignettes and it creates no answer cue, no shared key and no content redundancy. (2) MA-Q-0158 produces the single highest per-choice overlap in the entire bank, best single-choice Jaccard 0.889, arising solely from the recurrence of the statutory formula 'legitimate medical purpose ... usual course of professional practice' in its option E and this item's option B. That formula is a fixed legal phrase that necessarily recurs wherever prescription validity is examined, so its reappearance is unavoidable and correct rather than duplicative. The items are otherwise unrelated: MA-Q-0158 is a federal item in area 3 under rule FED-CII-MULTIPLE testing the multiple Schedule II prescription pathway, quantity limits and earliest-fill-date instructions; MA-Q-0288 is a Massachusetts item in area 2 testing which determinations 247 CMR 9.15(2) enumerates. They share no rule_id, no area, no topic and no subtopic, stem Jaccard is 0.000 and whole-item Jaccard is 0.137. (3) MA-Q-0162 and MA-Q-0163 are the nearest conceptual neighbours, both under 'Prescription validity' with rule FED-CORRESPONDING-RESP. Both are federal corresponding-responsibility items about resolving diversion red flags before a dispensing decision, that is about pharmacist conduct once suspicion arises. MA-Q-0288 asks the prior and different question of which determinations the Massachusetts regulation enumerates at all. Whole-item Jaccard is 0.080 and 0.133 respectively. No collision. Across the full bank the maximum whole-item Jaccard against any question is 0.137 and the maximum stem Jaccard is 0.071, there are no duplicate stems anywhere in the bank, no other question shares this item's family_id B3B_0288R1_MA_VALIDITY_VS_ADJACENT_DUTIES, and no other question contains any choice string identical to any of this item's five choices.

SUPPLEMENTAL B3-A R1 COMPARATORS AT c7b438f253089b74231e50040603458d46d20e6c. MA-Q-0241 (SATA, area 1, 'Pharmacy personnel' / 'Product-specific handling prohibition', rule MA-CII-SUPPORT-HANDLING, concerning a non-abuse-deterrent hydrocodone-only extended release product and support personnel handling) and MA-Q-0256 (SBA, area 1, 'Licensure' / 'Continuing education daily cap', rule MA-CE-ANNUAL-STRUCTURE) are both remote from this item. Whole-item Jaccard is 0.013 and 0.012, stem Jaccard is 0.000 for both, best single-choice Jaccard is 0.000 for both, and neither shares a rule_id, area, topic or subtopic with MA-Q-0288. Neither creates any future-production collision risk.

AUTHENTIC_DISTRACTORS, EXPLICIT PER-OPTION TREATMENT. Both incorrect options state genuine, currently effective Massachusetts obligations that a prepared candidate must actively rule out on legal grounds, which is the standard this criterion sets. Option A, that the prescriber holds a current Massachusetts Controlled Substances Registration: a prepared candidate could very plausibly credit this, and it is the stronger of the two distractors. The governing section is headed 'Verifying a Practitioner's Prescriptive Authority', so a candidate who recalls the heading rather than the enumerated text would expect prescriber-credential verification to be exactly what the section requires the pharmacist to determine. The MCSR is a real and heavily examined Massachusetts credential under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 7, Massachusetts pharmacists do attend to prescriber registration in practice, and the federal corresponding-responsibility framework trains candidates to associate prescriber authority with prescription validity. It is nonetheless wrong because registration verification is not one of the four determinations 247 CMR 9.15(2) enumerates, and within 247 CMR 9.00 the Massachusetts controlled substance registration language attaches to the pharmacy's own maintained documents under 247 CMR 9.19(8), not to any pharmacist determination. Option D, that the patient's history has been screened in the Prescription Monitoring Program: a prepared candidate could also very plausibly credit this. The monitoring-programme duty sits in the immediately preceding subsection, 247 CMR 9.15(1), which is maximal adjacency; MassPAT is highly salient in Massachusetts practice and candidates associate it with pre-dispensing workflow; and several other jurisdictions do impose pharmacist query duties before dispensing, so cross-jurisdictional transfer makes the proposition feel familiar. It is nonetheless wrong because 9.15(1) imposes registration and maintenance of login information, an access obligation, not a determination about the prescription in hand, and because M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 24A directs the utilisation requirement to participants issuing prescriptions while providing for pharmacists to be trained in the programme through continuing education. Neither incorrect option is absurd on its face, neither is a filler, and neither can be eliminated without knowing the boundary of the enumerated list. Correct options B, C and E are not merely plausible but verbatim restatements of 9.15(2)(a), (b) and (c), so the item discriminates on genuine knowledge of the enumeration.

WORDING_NOT_GUESSABLE, EXPLICIT TREATMENT. No surface strategy recovers the key. Length gives no signal in either direction: the correct set contains both the longest option, B at 136 characters and 21 words, and the shortest option, E at 35 characters and 5 words, while the two incorrect options are tightly clustered at 84 and 85 characters. The correct mean length, 75.7 characters, is lower than the incorrect mean, 84.5, so 'longest is correct' and 'shortest is filler' both fail. No option contains an absolute or hedging qualifier: a scan for always, never, only, solely, automatically, immediately, exclusively and all returned zero hits across all five options, so the classical eliminate-the-absolute heuristic yields nothing. All five options are grammatically parallel, each opening as a 'That ...' clause, so no option is a syntactic outlier and none is grammatically mismatched to the stem. The stem does not disclose how many options are correct, and the keyed count of three sits on the bank's modal SATA count, 56 of 112 SATA items key three options, so count-guessing gains nothing. The keyed combination BCE occurs 3 times among 112 SATA items and is not a positional outlier; SATA answer-position load across the bank is spread at A 22.4 percent, B 23.2, C 20.7, D 18.4 and E 15.3. The one surface pattern a test-wise candidate might notice, that the keyed options assert facts about the prescription and the treatment relationship while the rejected options assert external verification acts, is the substantive legal distinction the item is designed to test, namely determinations versus adjacent administrative duties, so exploiting it requires the underlying knowledge rather than substituting for it.

DISTINCT_FROM_BANK, EXPLICIT TREATMENT. Distinct on every measure applied across all 293 comparisons. The item is the sole occupant of its family_id, the sole occupant of its subtopic, and shares its topic with only MA-Q-0289, from which it is separated by question type, by rule focus and by the direction of the discrimination tested. Maximum whole-item overlap anywhere in the bank is 0.137 and maximum stem overlap is 0.071, both low. The single elevated per-choice figure, 0.889 against MA-Q-0158, is fully accounted for by a fixed statutory phrase and is not a content collision. No duplicate stem exists in the bank and no choice string is reused. The tested proposition, that 247 CMR 9.15(2) is a closed enumeration from which two genuinely adjacent Massachusetts duties are absent, is asked nowhere else in the bank.

STEM READING. The stem admits no second reasonable legal reading. 'The regulation' is uniquely fixed by the surrounding words 'requires of her professional judgment before any prescription may be filled', which track the operative language of 247 CMR 9.15(2) and match no competing Massachusetts provision. 'Among the determinations' is necessary and correctly drafted, because the fourth enumerated determination under 9.15(2)(d) is not offered as a choice; the stem therefore does not represent the offered set as exhaustive and cannot be attacked for the omission. 'Before any prescription may be filled' faithfully reproduces the unrestricted scope of 'may not fill a prescription' and does not improperly narrow the rule to controlled substances or improperly widen it beyond filling.

REMAINING CRITERIA. jurisprudence_reasoning: the item requires distinguishing the boundary of an enumerated regulatory list from obligations in the immediately surrounding subsections and section heading, which is reasoning about the scope of an enumeration rather than recall. practice_plausibility: a newly licensed pharmacist asking a preceptor what she must satisfy herself of before filling is an ordinary and realistic entry-of-practice exchange. reasoning_not_trivia: no number, date, threshold or list position is being recalled; the discrimination is which obligations are determinations at all. natural_rule_combination: MA-PRESCRIPTION-VALIDITY-DETERMINATION and MA-PMP-REGISTRATION-DUTY are adjacent subsections of the same section, 247 CMR 9.15(2) and 9.15(1), so combining them reproduces the structure of the regulation itself rather than assembling an artificial pairing. appropriate_drug_context: the rule is drug-agnostic, no drug is named, none is required, and drug_ids is correctly empty. not_schedule_flashcard: no schedule classification, schedule-specific limit or scheduling recall is involved anywhere in the item. public_style_without_copying: the vignette framing, the preceptor exchange and the distractor construction are original; the correct options necessarily track regulatory wording because they restate the enumerated determinations, which is proper restatement of public law and not reproduction of any published examination item.

COMPLETENESS CHECK. Consistent with the independence requirement, the legal and realism judgments recorded above were formed in full before any prior audit finding, repair rationale or old-hash history for MA-Q-0288 was consulted; the Phase-1 blind lock at commit b78ba8ae3b78852a90c92983c5f9b48084db407e independently produced the keyed set B, C, E and rejected A and D before the canonical record was opened. Only afterwards was the superseded item at hash 343520a4112cde0f746b9d4fb5062cc627d25438c3d94e312c5d97759a58bb68 and the prior CLAUDE-FRESH-B3B initial realism finding examined, solely to confirm that nothing previously identified remains unaddressed. That prior finding recorded REALISM FAIL, MINOR_EDIT, Medium, with authentic_distractors false, on two grounds: first, that under the superseded key the item's only incorrect option had no regulatory nexus and no prepared candidate would credit it, so the whole discriminating power rested on a single inauthentic distractor; second, that the superseded stem, which asked what remained to be determined after the prescriber had confirmed authorship by telephone, supported a second reasonable reading on which the authenticity determination had been discharged. Both defects are resolved in the item under review, and my independent analysis reached that conclusion on its own terms before the prior finding was read. The telephone-confirmation clause is gone, and the present stem asks the unconditioned question of what the regulation requires before any prescription may be filled, which as recorded above admits no second reasonable legal reading. The single inauthentic distractor is gone and has been replaced by two independently authentic ones, options A and D, each a genuine and currently effective Massachusetts obligation drawn from the section heading and from the immediately preceding subsection respectively, each analysed per-option above. The keyed set moved from four correct of five to three correct of five, so discriminating power now rests on two authentic rejections rather than one implausible one. No residual defect from the prior finding survives, and this review identifies no new defect. Contamination status CLEAN.

questions.stem: A newly hired Massachusetts pharmacist dispenses medications reported to the Prescription Monitoring Program. Her pharmacy holds an institutional MassPAT account that the Manager of Record administers. What does the regulation require of her personally?

choices.text: She shall register with and maintain login information for the monitoring system.
Nothing further, because the pharmacy's account covers all dispensing staff.
She must register only if she dispenses Schedule II controlled substances.
She must register within 30 days of her first Board disciplinary contact.
She must register only if the Manager of Record delegates monitoring duties to her.

explanation.core_reasoning: 247 CMR 9.15(1) requires a pharmacist who dispenses medications reported to the Massachusetts Prescription Monitoring Program to register with, and maintain login information for, the electronic system authorized by M.G.L. c. 94C, § 24A, known as PMP or MassPAT. The duty is personal and includes maintaining the login, not merely enrolling once.

choice_analysis.A: Correct: personal registration and maintained login information.
choice_analysis.B: A pharmacy-level account does not discharge the individual duty.
choice_analysis.C: The trigger is dispensing medications reported to the program, not a single schedule.
choice_analysis.D: The duty is not linked to disciplinary contact.
choice_analysis.E: The duty does not depend on delegation by the Manager of Record.

related_facts: The pharmacist must separately make the four validity determinations before filling.
explanation.mpje_trap: An institutional account does not satisfy a duty the regulation places on the dispensing pharmacist.

reasoning_steps: Identify the trigger as dispensing medications reported to the program
Attach the duty to the individual pharmacist
Include maintaining login information, not only initial registration

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy offers a nursing home's administrator free catering for staff events. Nothing is said about individual patients, but the pharmacy hopes the facility will send it more business. How does the regulation treat the arrangement?

choices.text: Permitted, because no referral of any individual patient is being solicited.
Permitted, because catering is not a payment of money.
Permitted if the facility discloses the arrangement to its residents.
Permitted if the value stays below the pharmacy's ordinary annual marketing budget.
Prohibited, because a licensee may not offer anything of value for the generation of business.

explanation.core_reasoning: 247 CMR 9.01(11) bars a licensee from offering, soliciting or receiving remuneration or anything of value to or from any person who owns, operates, manages or is an employee of a hospital, nursing home or other health care facility in return for a referral or for the generation of business from the sale or furnishing of drugs, devices or services to such persons or institutions.

choice_analysis.A: Generation of business is covered separately from an individual referral.
choice_analysis.B: Anything of value is covered, not only money.
choice_analysis.C: Disclosure is not a stated cure.
choice_analysis.D: No de minimis or budget-based exception is provided.
choice_analysis.E: Correct: offering anything of value for the generation of business is prohibited.

related_facts: The prohibition runs in both directions, covering offering as well as receiving.
explanation.mpje_trap: The rule does not require a named patient or a cash payment; generation of business and anything of value suffice.

reasoning_steps: Identify the recipient as a manager of a health care facility
Classify the catering as anything of value
Apply the generation-of-business limb rather than looking for a named patient

questions.stem: A Massachusetts clinic pharmacy that does not hold a Drug Store pharmacy licence is asked to fill a prescription for the adult sibling of a clinic employee. The sibling lives across town and is not a clinic patient. May the pharmacist dispense?

choices.text: No, because the permitted recipients do not extend to that relative.
Yes, because the family members of employees are always covered.
Yes, provided the prescription was written by a clinic practitioner.
Yes, provided the sibling pays the usual and customary retail price.
Yes, because the restriction applies only to controlled substances.

explanation.core_reasoning: 247 CMR 9.01(13) provides that, unless otherwise permitted by law, a pharmacist connected with a hospital or clinic pharmacy that does not hold a Drug Store pharmacy licence may not dispense to any person other than inpatients or outpatients of the hospital or clinic, employees of that institution, or those employees' spouses and children who live in the same house. An adult sibling living elsewhere is outside that class.

choice_analysis.A: Correct: the permitted class does not include an employee's sibling living elsewhere.
choice_analysis.B: The family limb is confined to spouses and children living in the same house.
choice_analysis.C: The identity of the prescriber does not extend the permitted class.
choice_analysis.D: Payment terms are irrelevant to the restriction.
choice_analysis.E: The restriction is not limited to controlled substances.

related_facts: Inpatients and outpatients of the hospital or clinic remain within the permitted class.
explanation.mpje_trap: The family limb is narrow: spouses and children in the same house, not relatives generally.

reasoning_steps: Confirm the institution lacks a Drug Store pharmacy licence
List the permitted recipient classes
Place the adult sibling outside those classes

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy arranges a sequence of transfers so that a patient ends up holding a supply the pharmacy could not lawfully have dispensed to him directly. Each transfer in the sequence, taken on its own, complies with the governing rules, and every step is documented. How should the arrangement be assessed?

choices.text: No violation arises, because each step in the sequence independently complies.
No violation arises, because the prohibition reaches only direct circumvention.
A violation arises if the Board shows the patient was harmed by the supply.
A violation arises if the pharmacy gained financially from the arrangement.
A violation arises, because the manner was designed to circumvent the law.

explanation.core_reasoning: 247 CMR 9.01(2) bars a licensee from processing a prescription, dispensing a drug, device or other substance, or administering a controlled substance or vaccine in a manner intended, either directly or INDIRECTLY, to circumvent any law or regulation governing the practice of pharmacy. The standard attaches to the manner and its design, so the lawfulness of each individual step is not the question.

choice_analysis.A: Step-wise compliance does not answer a prohibition aimed at the design of the whole.
choice_analysis.B: Indirect circumvention is expressly within the prohibition.
choice_analysis.C: Patient harm is not an element of the standard.
choice_analysis.D: Financial gain is not an element of the standard.
choice_analysis.E: Correct: the manner was intended to reach indirectly what could not be done directly.

related_facts: The prohibition covers processing, dispensing and administering alike
explanation.mpje_trap: Candidates audit each step for legality and conclude that a chain of lawful steps must itself be lawful.

reasoning_steps: Identify what the pharmacy could not lawfully do directly
Ask whether the arrangement was designed to reach that result
Apply the indirect limb of 247 CMR 9.01(2) to the manner rather than to each step

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy has prescription pads printed with its own name and address and supplies them free of charge to a nearby prescriber. questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy is asked about a dispensing from last year. Its records contain no entry that the patient failed to accept the pharmacist's offer to counsel, and no entry that counselling was actually given. What follows from that state of the records?

choices.text: Nothing follows; the records are simply silent about what happened that day.
A presumption arises that the counselling was provided to that patient.
A presumption arises that the counselling was not provided to that patient.
The pharmacy must instead produce the dispensing pharmacist's recollection.
The pharmacy is in breach, because counselling must be affirmatively recorded.

explanation.core_reasoning: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 21A provides that THE ABSENCE OF ANY RECORD OF A FAILURE TO ACCEPT THE PHARMACIST'S OFFER TO COUNSEL SHALL CREATE A PRESUMPTION THAT SUCH COUNSELING WAS PROVIDED. The statute makes silence work in the pharmacist's favour, which is the reverse of the usual documentation intuition.

choice_analysis.A: The statute attaches a specific consequence to that silence.
choice_analysis.B: Correct: silence creates a presumption that counselling was provided.
choice_analysis.C: This inverts the statutory presumption.
choice_analysis.D: No recollection evidence is required to raise the presumption.
choice_analysis.E: The statute requires recording a failure to accept, not an affirmative record of counselling.

related_facts: The information may be recorded in the profile, the signature log or any other system of records
explanation.mpje_trap: Candidates apply the general documentation instinct that an unrecorded act is an unproven act.

reasoning_steps: Identify what the statute says must be recorded, which is a failure to accept
Note that no such record exists here
Apply the presumption the statute attaches to that absence

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist is reviewing a proposed collaborative practice agreement before signing it. Which features does the statutory definition require for the agreement to be validly constituted? Select all that apply.

The collaborative practice may extend beyond the supervising physician's own scope.
It is subject to review and renewal on a biennial basis.
It must be filed with the Board before the pharmacist may act under it.
It must include individually developed guidelines for any prescriptive practice.

explanation.core_reasoning: A collaborative practice agreement is defined by statute as a written and signed agreement between a pharmacist with relevant training and experience and a supervising physician. The collaborative practice must sit within the scope of the supervising physician's practice, each agreement is subject to review and renewal on a biennial basis, and individually developed guidelines are required for any prescriptive practice.

choice_analysis.A: Correct: written and signed.
choice_analysis.B: The statute requires the collaborative practice to sit within the supervising physician's scope.
choice_analysis.C: Correct: biennial review and renewal.
choice_analysis.D: Filing with the Board is not part of the statutory definition.
choice_analysis.E: Correct: individually developed prescriptive guidelines are required.

related_facts: 247 CMR 16.04(6) separately governs where the agreement must be held

Separate what the definition requires from what a pharmacist might assume
Note the currency requirement that keeps the agreement effective

questions.stem: Two Massachusetts pharmacists reach opposite conclusions on the same drug utilization review question. One relies on a current peer-reviewed journal article that is not among the works named in the regulation. The other relies on a superseded edition of a compendium that is named. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

The journal article may properly be relied upon as peer-reviewed literature.
Neither may be relied upon, since only the named works are acceptable sources.
The superseded edition remains acceptable, because the compendium is named.
The superseded edition fails, because the review must rest on current standards.

choice_analysis.C: The list is not exhaustive.
choice_analysis.D: Being named does not cure a lack of currency.

questions.stem: During prospective review a Massachusetts pharmacist identifies a therapeutic duplication, telephones the prescriber, agrees a change to the therapy, and dispenses the revised prescription. She makes no note of the call, on the basis that the clinical issue was fully resolved before anything was dispensed. What remains outstanding?

A report of the therapeutic duplication to the Board of Registration in Pharmacy.
A second prospective review of the revised therapy before it is dispensed.
Written confirmation from the prescriber of the change that was agreed.
Documentation of the measures she took in response to the review.

explanation.core_reasoning: 247 CMR 9.17(2) leaves the choice of responsive measure open, offering consultation with the prescriber or with the patient as examples, but then provides that a pharmacist SHALL DOCUMENT ANY MEASURES TAKEN in response to a drug utilization review. The documentation duty is unconditional and is not discharged by resolving the underlying problem.

choice_analysis.B: No report to the Board is required.
choice_analysis.C: No second review is required by the paragraph.
choice_analysis.D: Written prescriber confirmation is not what the paragraph requires.

Note that the pharmacist did take an appropriate measure

questions.stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacy that holds the equipment and the ingredients turns away a request for a simple non-sterile oral suspension that is customary in its community, telling the parent it prefers not to compound. Later the same day it declines a request for a sterile preparation. How should the two refusals be assessed?

choices.text: Both are permitted, since compounding is a service a pharmacy may choose to offer.
Both are prohibited, since a licensee may not refuse to compound on preference.
The first refusal is permitted and the second refusal is prohibited on these facts.
The first refusal is prohibited and the second falls outside the duty entirely.
Both turn on whether another nearby pharmacy could have compounded them instead.

explanation.core_reasoning: 247 CMR 9.01(15) provides that a licensee may not refuse to compound SIMPLE OR MODERATE NON-STERILE compounded preparations customary to the community needs, except upon extenuating circumstances or by a waiver of Board regulation. A preference not to offer the service is neither. The duty does not extend to sterile preparations, so the second refusal is outside it.

choice_analysis.A: The regulation makes customary non-sterile compounding a duty rather than an option.
choice_analysis.B: The duty does not reach sterile preparations.
choice_analysis.C: This reverses the analysis of the two requests.
choice_analysis.D: Correct: the duty catches the first request and does not reach the second.
choice_analysis.E: The availability of another pharmacy is not one of the two stated exceptions.

related_facts: The two exceptions are extenuating circumstances and a waiver of Board regulation
explanation.mpje_trap: Candidates treat compounding as a commercial service the pharmacy is free to decline.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist arranges a dispensing record so that a reviewer will draw a conclusion the pharmacist knows to be untrue. Every individual entry is literally accurate, no dispensing rule is broken, and in the event no one relies on the record and no loss is suffered by anyone. What is the position?

No violation, because no separate dispensing rule was broken by the pharmacist.

A violation if the Board shows a reviewer actually relied on the arrangement.
A violation if the arrangement produced some financial gain for the pharmacy.

The discriminating work is done by option D, whether the published list is closed or illustrative, and option E, whether administration is compulsory, both of which are judgments rather than recall, so reasoning_not_trivia is satisfied even though options A to C require knowledge of the list itself. Distractors are authentic: generalising from named products to their pharmacological class is the error the circular's own 'only medications eligible' wording is designed to prevent. TRANCHE-LEVEL OBSERVATIONS, recorded once here for the controller rather than against each item. (1) Distribution is healthy. All 35 items sit in area 2 across 23 rule records, 12 carrying a two-item pair and 11 a single item; SBA key positions run A4 B3 C3 D6 E5 over 21 items, which is well balanced and does not repeat the E-heavy concentration flagged in BATCH3-B3B; SATA cardinality runs 2 six times, 3 five times and 4 three times, in line with the 152-item SATA bank. (2) No duplication. Maximum lexical overlap against the whole 406-record bank is 0.28 Jaccard and every top neighbour is an intended same-family sibling. The three places where a tranche item shares a rule record or statutory paragraph with an existing bank item are all complementary rather than repetitive: MA-Q-0311 with MA-Q-0371 on constitution versus currency, MA-Q-0322 with MA-Q-0323 on the exception versus the rest period, and MA-Q-0340 and MA-Q-0341 with MA-Q-0082, MA-Q-0083 and MA-Q-0084 on different limbs of M.G.L. c. 112, s. 24B1/2(c)(5). That paragraph now carries five bank items, which is the densest concentration on any single provision and is worth watching before more are added, but no two of the five ask the same question. (3) A construction signature runs across the four-correct SATA items. In MA-Q-0328, MA-Q-0346 and MA-Q-0359 the single incorrect option is in each case the one that over-generalises, adds an external gate, or asserts uniformity, while every specific, hedged option is keyed correct. A candidate who learns the heuristic 'reject the sweeping option and take the rest' recovers the exact key in all three without reading the authority. MA-Q-0359 is failed on this ground because there the heuristic is sufficient on its own; MA-Q-0328 and MA-Q-0346 survive only because their remaining options still carry content that has to be known. The set would be stronger if at least one four-correct item placed a plausible, specifically worded error among the options instead of relying on a blanket statement to carry the distractor role. (4) Two items are failed for a mis-keyed correct option, MA-Q-0340 option E and MA-Q-0348 option D. Both errors run the same way: a correct statement of a regulation has been recorded as a distractor on a reading that adds a condition the option does not contain. In each case the item contradicts its own governing rule record, and in MA-Q-0340 it also contradicts sibling item MA-Q-0344 in this same tranche. Whatever process produced these two should be checked against the rest of B3-D before release, since the failure mode is a systematic one rather than a slip.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts collaborative practice agreement authorises the pharmacist to modify the dosage of a named medication for a referred patient. questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy's computerized system cannot show what it previously dispensed to a patient until an overnight batch runs, so at the counter the pharmacist cannot see the patient's earlier fills. The system must allow immediate retrieval when the prescription is presented.
A pharmacy may rely on the overnight batch if it documents the limitation.
Institutional sterile compounding pharmacies are outside these requirements.

choice_analysis.B: The reasonable-effort standard qualifies the content duty only.

choice_analysis.D: Documenting a limitation does not satisfy an unqualified requirement.
choice_analysis.E: Correct: the section does not apply to them.

explanation.mpje_trap: Candidates carry the reasonable-effort standard across the whole paragraph and excuse a system that cannot retrieve in time.

Apply the immediate-retrieval requirement to the batch delay

questions.stem: A Massachusetts collaborative practice agreement was properly written, signed and within the supervising physician's scope when it was made twenty-six months ago. Neither party has reviewed it since. The pharmacist proposes to keep co-managing referred patients while a review is scheduled. What is the position?

The agreement stands, provided the pharmacist documents that a review is pending.
The agreement stands until the supervising physician gives notice of termination.
The agreement is out of currency, because review and renewal fall due biennially.
The agreement is void, and every act taken under it in month 25 must be reported.

explanation.core_reasoning: The M.G.L. c. 112, s. 24B1/2(a) definition provides that each collaborative practice agreement SHALL BE SUBJECT TO REVIEW AND RENEWAL ON A BIENNIAL BASIS. Valid constitution at the outset does not keep an agreement current; the biennial review is a continuing condition, and twenty-six months without one leaves the agreement outside it.

choice_analysis.A: Currency is a separate requirement from constitution.
choice_analysis.B: A pending review is not a review.
choice_analysis.C: Termination by the physician is a different event from lapse of currency.
choice_analysis.D: Correct: the biennial review and renewal condition has not been met.

related_facts: The agreement must also include individually developed prescriptive guidelines
explanation.mpje_trap: Candidates check the formation requirements, find them satisfied, and never ask whether the instrument is still current.

reasoning_steps: Confirm the agreement was validly constituted
Apply the separate biennial review and renewal condition
Measure the elapsed period against it

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy makes its offer to counsel by printing a line on the receipt inviting the patient to ask for the pharmacist. Its manager says the statute leaves the method open so long as the patient learns the offer is available. A second patient that day is deaf and cannot use the telephone. What does the statute provide?

choices.text: Any method reaching the patient qualifies, so the receipt line is sufficient.
The offer is made face to face or by telephone, with an alternative where needs require.
The offer must be made face to face in every case, so the telephone is not available.
A printed offer qualifies where the pharmacy also posts a patient rights sign.
The pharmacy may decline to counsel the second patient because of the barrier.

explanation.core_reasoning: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 21A provides that the offer shall be made EITHER by face to face communication between the pharmacist or the pharmacist's designee and the patient, OR by telephone, EXCEPT WHEN THE PATIENT'S NEEDS OR AVAILABILITY REQUIRE AN ALTERNATIVE METHOD. The named methods are the rule and the alternative is a needs-driven exception, not a general licence.

choice_analysis.A: The statute names the methods rather than leaving them open.
choice_analysis.B: Correct: two named methods plus a needs-driven alternative.
choice_analysis.C: The telephone is expressly available.
choice_analysis.D: The rights sign is a separate requirement and does not change the method.
choice_analysis.E: A patient's needs open the alternative method rather than excusing the offer.

related_facts: A designee may make the offer, though only a pharmacist or intern may counsel
explanation.mpje_trap: Candidates read the exception as making every method acceptable, when it is available only where the patient's needs or availability require it.

reasoning_steps: Read the two methods the statute names
Read the exception and note that it is triggered by the patient's needs or availability
Apply it to the deaf patient rather than treating the barrier as an excuse

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy's label printer fails on a Saturday afternoon with patients waiting. The pharmacist writes labels by hand, in clear block capitals, for the remainder of the shift and again on Monday because the queue is long, although the printer was repaired that morning. How should the two days be assessed?

Saturday fails as well, unless the Board approved the handwriting in advance.
Monday is permitted, because a queue is itself an emergency for this purpose.

Saturday's printer failure opens the exception; Monday's workload does not, because the equipment was working.

choice_analysis.A: Correct: the exception is tied to the failure and to its period.
choice_analysis.B: Legibility is a condition of the exception, not a substitute for it.
choice_analysis.C: The regulation expressly provides for the failure case.
choice_analysis.D: No advance Board approval is contemplated.
choice_analysis.E: A queue is not a printing or equipment failure.

related_facts: The computerized pharmacy system is separately required for processing and profiles
explanation.mpje_trap: Candidates read legibility as the whole test and forget the exception has a trigger.

reasoning_steps: Identify whether a printing or equipment failure existed on each day
Confine the exception to the emergency period
Treat workload as outside the trigger

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist dispenses a product distributed solely under its generic name. The package carries no NDC number. The pharmacist can see the manufacturer's name on the carton and also has the repacker's name on the invoice. What must be recorded in the computerized pharmacy system?

The repacker's name, which is the entity that supplied this pharmacy.
Both names, so that the chain of supply is recorded in full.
The manufacturer's name, the repacker being a later fallback.
Neither name; the pharmacist records the generic name and strength.

explanation.core_reasoning: 247 CMR 9.04(7) sets an ordered fallback. Where a drug has been distributed solely under a generic name the pharmacist records the NDC number; if none exists, the NAME OF THE MANUFACTURER; and only IF THE MANUFACTURER'S NAME IS NOT AVAILABLE, the name of the distributor, packer or repacker. The manufacturer's name being available, it is the one to record.

choice_analysis.A: The regulation ranks the options rather than offering a choice.
choice_analysis.B: The repacker is reached only when the manufacturer's name is unavailable.
choice_analysis.C: The regulation calls for one identifier, taken in order.
choice_analysis.D: Correct: the manufacturer's name is the next step after the NDC.
choice_analysis.E: The generic name is what triggers the requirement, not what satisfies it.

related_facts: The record is made in the computerized pharmacy system
explanation.mpje_trap: Candidates treat the listed identifiers as alternatives rather than as a ranked sequence.

reasoning_steps: Confirm the drug was distributed solely under a generic name
Work down the fallback chain in order
Stop at the first available identifier

questions.stem: A Massachusetts prescription was written on 1 March. A patient presents it and the pharmacist must decide whether it is still within a thirty-day window. Which date is the last day on which it remains within date?

explanation.core_reasoning: 247 CMR 9.04(10) provides that in order to determine whether a prescription is within date a pharmacist shall count THE DAY AFTER THE PRESCRIPTION WAS WRITTEN AS DAY ONE. With 1 March as the date written, 2 March is day one, so day thirty is 31 March.

choice_analysis.A: That counts the date of issue as day one, which the regulation excludes.
choice_analysis.B: Correct: day one is 2 March, so the thirtieth day is 31 March.
choice_analysis.C: The regulation fixes the start precisely rather than disregarding a day.
choice_analysis.D: Only the date written is excluded, not the final day.
choice_analysis.E: The counting convention is general and does not vary by schedule.

related_facts: The length of the window is set by the provision governing that drug
explanation.mpje_trap: Candidates start counting on the date the prescription was written, which shifts every boundary by a day.

Count forward the length of the period
Note that the convention does not vary by schedule

The pharmacist's own note of the emergency completes what the regulation asks of the pharmacy.
The date, hour and nature of the emergency must be recorded on the prescription or in the pharmacy system.
The purchaser must indicate acceptance of the deviation in writing.
The deviation runs only toward the cheaper product, never toward the brand as written.

choice_analysis.B: The pharmacist's record is one of two conditions; the purchaser's written acceptance is the other.
choice_analysis.C: Correct: date, hour and nature, on the prescription or in the system.
choice_analysis.D: Correct: the purchaser indicates acceptance of the deviation in writing.

related_facts: The prescriptions are to be clearly identifiable and available for inspection
explanation.mpje_trap: Candidates stop at the permission and miss that the deviation is conditioned on a purchaser signature as well as a pharmacy record.

Match the direction of the deviation to which product is missing from stock
Apply both conditions, the pharmacy's record and the purchaser's written acceptance

questions.stem: A patient asks a Massachusetts pharmacy to set up her medications in a reusable weekly planner. She brings in a sealed, in-date bottle of her lisinopril that a pharmacy across town dispensed last month, and asks that it go in alongside the medications this pharmacy supplies. The pharmacy has a designated preparation space and written planner procedures. What should the pharmacist do about the lisinopril?

choices.text: Include it, since the patient requested the planner service and the bottle is sealed and in date.
Decline to place it in the planner, because it was dispensed by a different pharmacy.
Include it after transferring the original prescription to this pharmacy on the spot.
Include it once the patient signs an acknowledgement that she supplied the product.
Include it, provided the planner is labelled to show which pharmacy supplied each drug.

explanation.core_reasoning: 247 CMR 9.07 lets a pharmacy dispense medications in a reusable daily dosage planner at the patient's or the patient's agent's request, but the first condition is flat: a pharmacy may not place any medication in a reusable daily dosage planner that was previously dispensed by a different pharmacy. The condition is about where the product has already been, so a fresh transfer, a consent form or a label cannot reach back and cure it.

choice_analysis.A: The patient's request opens the service; it does not lift the provenance condition.
choice_analysis.B: Correct: 247 CMR 9.07(1) forbids placing another pharmacy's previously dispensed medication in the planner.
choice_analysis.C: Transferring the prescription governs future fills. This physical product has already been dispensed elsewhere.
choice_analysis.D: No acknowledgement is offered as a cure for the provenance condition.
choice_analysis.E: Labelling does not answer the objection, which is to the product's origin rather than to its identification.

related_facts: The pharmacy must also maintain cleaning, labeling, dispensing and hand hygiene procedures
explanation.mpje_trap: The sealed, in-date bottle invites a clinical judgment. The regulation asks a provenance question instead, and answers it without reference to the product's condition.

reasoning_steps: Confirm the planner service was requested by the patient or her agent
Identify which pharmacy previously dispensed each product offered for the planner
Apply the provenance condition before the housekeeping conditions

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy prepares multi-drug single-dose compliance packages. The pharmacy has a designated space, full written procedures for this packaging type, and a compatible package component. What controls whether the tablet may be included?

choices.text: The prescriber's request, since compliance packaging is prepared on the prescriber's direction.
The pharmacy's written procedures, since the regulation asks for procedures rather than outcomes.
The patient's informed acceptance of any reduction in shelf life.
The FDA-approved labeling, which the packaging must not contradict.
The Board's Schedule II and III maintenance-medication policy.

explanation.core_reasoning: 247 CMR 9.08(1) lists the conditions on compliance packaging together. Alongside the designated space, the written procedures and the compatibility requirement sits the condition that the compliance packaging not conflict with the USP-DI monograph or FDA-approved labeling. choice_analysis.A: A prescriber may ask, but 247 CMR 9.08 conditions what the pharmacy may do.
choice_analysis.B: Procedures are one condition among several and do not displace the labeling condition.
choice_analysis.C: Patient acceptance is not among the conditions the regulation lists.
choice_analysis.D: Correct: the packaging may not conflict with the USP-DI monograph or FDA-approved labeling.
choice_analysis.E: That policy governs which controlled substances may be included, not moisture-sensitive product handling.

related_facts: The regulation also requires that the medications be compatible with each other and with the packaging
explanation.mpje_trap: Two plausible authorities are in the room, a prescriber and the pharmacy's own procedures. The condition that decides the case is the product's own approved labeling.

reasoning_steps: Separate the regulation's conditions from the Board's controlled-substance policy
Read the FDA-approved labeling for a storage direction
Treat a labeling conflict as decisive rather than as a factor to be weighed

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy is commissioning an automated system that counts tablets, fills vials and applies labels. To keep cells full, the pharmacy plans to top up a cell without emptying it first, so two manufacturer lot numbers will sit together. Which statements about this arrangement are correct? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Comingling lot numbers in one cell is prohibited outright.
The pharmacy must hold a policy to quarantine all comingled lots if a single lot is recalled.
A pharmacist's visual check of the finished vial satisfies the verification requirement.
Controlled substance accountability need not be addressed until the system handles Schedule II drugs.
The system must use a technological verification such as bar code, weight or RFID checking.

explanation.core_reasoning: 247 CMR 9.11(1) permits pharmacy processing automation to count, fill and label on two conditions: the automation uses a technological verification -- bar code, electronic, weight, radio frequency identification or similar -- to ensure the correct medication is dispensed; and, if lot numbers are comingled in a single cell, the pharmacy maintains a policy and procedure to quarantine all comingled lot numbers in the event a single lot is recalled. 247 CMR 9.11(2) requires standing policies covering operation and maintenance, security, controlled substance accountability, quality assurance, and stocking and return activities.

choice_analysis.A: Comingling is permitted; it is conditioned on a quarantine policy rather than forbidden.
choice_analysis.B: Correct: the quarantine policy is what makes comingling permissible.
choice_analysis.C: The regulation asks for a technological verification, which a visual check is not.
choice_analysis.D: Controlled substance accountability is a standing policy requirement, not one triggered by schedule.
choice_analysis.E: Correct: the named examples are bar code, electronic, weight and RFID verification.

related_facts: A licensed pharmacist remains responsible for final dispensing process validation under 247 CMR 9.04(1)
explanation.mpje_trap: The comingling plan reads like a violation looking for a penalty. The regulation permits it and asks instead what happens on the day a lot is recalled.

reasoning_steps: Identify the two conditions that permit the automation at all
Recognise comingling as a conditioned practice rather than a prohibited one
Keep the standing policy requirements separate from the two permissive conditions

The arrangement works, because the pharmacy's procedures cover accountability and security.
The arrangement works if the practice registers the cabinet with the Board separately.

Confirm whether the host site is a licensed health care facility

choice_analysis.D: The fee point is right, but the pharmacy may act as her agent rather than leaving it to her.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacy dispenses a Schedule II opioid for a patient who lives in a long-term care facility, delivered to the facility for her use there. A technician asks whether the state consumer educational pamphlet on narcotic drugs must go out with it. What is the correct answer?

choices.text: Yes, because the pamphlet duty attaches to every Schedule II narcotic dispensing.
Yes, unless the facility confirms in writing that it will counsel the resident itself.
No, because delivery to a facility is not a dispensing to a consumer.
No, because the pamphlet is required only for a first fill of a given opioid.
No, because the patient is a resident of a long-term care facility.

explanation.core_reasoning: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 21 requires a pharmacist to distribute the pamphlet when dispensing a narcotic or controlled substance contained in Schedule II or III, and then states three situations in which pharmacists are not required to distribute it: the patient is receiving outpatient palliative care under c. 111, s. 227; the patient is a resident of a long-term care facility; or the drug is prescribed for use in the treatment of substance use disorder or opioid dependence. The second exception answers this case on its face.

choice_analysis.A: The general duty is subject to three statutory exceptions.
choice_analysis.B: The statute does not condition the exception on any undertaking by the facility.
choice_analysis.C: The dispensing is still a dispensing; the exception turns on the patient's residence.
choice_analysis.D: Section 21 draws no distinction between a first fill and a later one.
choice_analysis.E: Correct: residence in a long-term care facility is one of the three named exceptions.

related_facts: The department distributes the pamphlets to pharmacies, not including institutional pharmacies
explanation.mpje_trap: Two of the wrong answers reach the right result by the wrong route, which is worth as little as the wrong result when the next patient does not fit that route.

reasoning_steps: Confirm the drug is a Schedule II or III narcotic or controlled substance
Run the three statutory exceptions before concluding the pamphlet is due
Match the facts to the exception that actually fits

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy licensed for sterile compounding prepares two products on the same morning: a sterile infusion for an outpatient, and a sterile preparation for a patient admitted as an inpatient in the same hospital under its institutional licence. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Both containers must be labelled as a sterile compounded preparation.
The outpatient container must also carry the pharmacist-contact telephone number.
The telephone must be staffed during regular hours of operation and at least 56 hours a week.
The inpatient preparation must also carry the telephone number, since the pharmacy does sterile compounding.
The pharmacist reachable on that number must have access to the patient's records.

explanation.core_reasoning: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 21 sets two distinct duties. All drug preparations compounded by a board-licensed pharmacy must carry a label notifying users and practitioners that the drug is a sterile or non-sterile compounded preparation. Separately, pharmacies engaged in sterile or complex non-sterile compounding must provide a telephone number fostering communication between patients and a pharmacist employed by the pharmacy who has access to the patient's records, staffed during regular hours of operation every day and not less than 56 hours per week, affixed to the container alongside the compounded-preparation label. That telephone paragraph does not apply to an institutional pharmacy licensed under c. 112, s. 39I where the sterile preparation is to be administered to an inpatient within the same hospital.

choice_analysis.A: Correct: the compounded-preparation label duty reaches all such preparations.
choice_analysis.B: Correct: the outpatient container falls squarely within the telephone paragraph.
choice_analysis.C: Correct: staffed during regular hours every day and not less than 56 hours per week.
choice_analysis.D: The telephone paragraph is disapplied for an inpatient preparation within the same hospital.
choice_analysis.E: Correct: the pharmacist reached must have access to the patient's records.

related_facts: The carve-out is tied to administration within the same hospital, not merely to inpatient status
explanation.mpje_trap: One exception is written into one of the two paragraphs. Reading it as an exception to both strips the required compounded-preparation label from the inpatient container.

reasoning_steps: Separate the compounded-preparation label duty from the telephone-number duty
Apply the institutional inpatient carve-out to the telephone duty only
Check the staffing standard attached to the telephone number

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist is dispensing a Schedule II opioid prescribed for a 15-year-old patient. The patient's mother is collecting the medication. The pharmacist has already explained the potential adverse risks of the opioid. What does the statute require next?

choices.text: Nothing further, because a minor cannot be dispensed an opioid antagonist.
Offer to dispense an opioid antagonist to the mother as the minor's parent.
Offer to dispense an opioid antagonist only if the prescriber has also ordered one.
Obtain the prescriber's authorisation before raising an opioid antagonist with the family.
Record that the patient is a minor and treat the antagonist offer as inapplicable.

explanation.core_reasoning: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18D(b) requires a pharmacist dispensing an opioid contained in Schedule II to inform the patient of the potential adverse risks of the prescription opioid and to offer to dispense an opioid antagonist to the patient, and where applicable to a designee of the patient, or, for a patient who is a minor, to the minor's parent or guardian. The statute routes the offer to the parent or guardian rather than removing it.

choice_analysis.A: The statute redirects the offer for a minor; it does not withdraw it.
choice_analysis.B: Correct: for a minor patient the offer is made to the minor's parent or guardian.
choice_analysis.C: Section 18D states no condition based on a separate order from the prescriber.
choice_analysis.D: The duty is the pharmacist's own and is not gated on prescriber authorisation.
choice_analysis.E: Minority changes who receives the offer, not whether one is made.

related_facts: The duty is to offer; the patient or family need not accept or purchase an antagonist
explanation.mpje_trap: Minority reads like a reason the duty falls away. The statute treats it as a reason the offer goes to someone else.

reasoning_steps: Confirm the drug is an opioid contained in Schedule II
Identify the correct recipient of the offer for this patient
Keep the offer duty separate from any dispensing that may follow

questions.stem: A Massachusetts patient presents a Schedule II oxycodone prescription written by her Massachusetts physician nine days earlier. She asks the pharmacy to dispense only part of it today and to hold the balance. A colleague says the initial partial fill is already too late because it is past the fifth day after the issue date. Which assessment is correct?

choices.text: The colleague is right; the five-day limit runs from the issue date for any Schedule II partial fill.
The colleague is right, but only because the drug is a narcotic rather than a stimulant.
The colleague is wrong; the five-day limit reaches only prescriptions filled on the out-of-state pathways.
The colleague is wrong; no deadline governs a patient-requested partial fill of a Schedule II prescription.
The colleague is wrong; the five-day limit runs from the first dispensing rather than from the issue date.

explanation.core_reasoning: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4) contains two deadlines with different reach. The remaining portion must be filled not later than 30 days after the prescription issue date. The five-day limit on the initial partial dispensing applies only to a prescription filled pursuant to subsection (d) or (d1/2) -- respectively a nonnarcotic Schedule II prescription issued by an out-of-state practitioner, and a narcotic Schedule II prescription issued by a practitioner registered in Maine or a contiguous state. This prescription came from a Massachusetts physician, so neither pathway is engaged and the initial partial fill on day nine is in time.

choice_analysis.A: The five-day limit is conditioned on the prescription having been filled under s. 18(d) or (d1/2).
choice_analysis.B: The narcotic distinction separates (d) from (d1/2); both remain out-of-state pathways.
choice_analysis.C: Correct: subsections (d) and (d1/2) are the out-of-state prescriber pathways.
choice_analysis.D: The 30-day remainder deadline still governs, measured from the issue date.
choice_analysis.E: Both deadlines in the subsection are measured from the prescription issue date.

related_facts: Only the pharmacy that dispensed the lesser quantity may dispense the remaining portion
explanation.mpje_trap: The five-day figure is real and sits in the same subsection, which makes it easy to apply to a prescription the subsection never sends down that path.

reasoning_steps: Identify where the prescription was issued and under which subsection it is filled
Match each deadline in s. 18(d3/4) to the pathway it governs
Measure the surviving deadline from the prescription issue date

questions.stem: A prescriber telephones a pharmacy about a drug for which FDA requires a Medication Guide. She has concluded that receiving the Guide would not be in this particular patient's best interest, and directs that it not be provided. At the counter the patient asks the pharmacist for written information about the medicine. What must the pharmacist do?

choices.text: Provide the Medication Guide, because the patient has requested information.
Withhold the Guide but supply the manufacturer's patient information leaflet instead.
Withhold the Guide, because the prescriber's clinical direction controls at the counter.
Withhold the Guide unless the patient puts the request in writing.
Contact the prescriber for permission before providing anything in writing.

explanation.core_reasoning: 21 CFR 208.26(b) permits the prescribing practitioner who determines that a Medication Guide is not in a particular patient's best interest to direct that it not be provided to that patient. The same paragraph then states that the authorized dispenser shall provide a Medication Guide to any patient who requests information when the drug product is dispensed, regardless of any such direction by the licensed practitioner. The patient's request at the counter is the trigger, and it overrides the direction.

choice_analysis.A: Correct: a request from the patient overrides the prescriber's direction.
choice_analysis.B: The regulation names the Medication Guide, not a substitute document.
choice_analysis.C: The direction stands only until the patient asks for information.
choice_analysis.D: Nothing in 208.26(b) requires the request to be in writing.
choice_analysis.E: The regulation resolves the conflict itself and does not route it back to the prescriber.

related_facts: Without a request, the practitioner's direction is effective for that patient
explanation.mpje_trap: The prescriber's direction is lawful, which makes it tempting to treat as final. The same paragraph that grants it also takes it away the moment the patient asks.

reasoning_steps: Confirm the product is one for which a Medication Guide is required
Note the prescriber's direction and the authority that permits it
Apply the patient-request override in the same paragraph

questions.stem: A neighbour collects a prescription on behalf of a housebound patient. The product is one for which FDA requires a Medication Guide. The pharmacy's practice is to hold the Guide on file and give it to the patient at the next visit, on the view that the Guide belongs to the patient personally. What is the correct assessment of that practice?

choices.text: It is sound, because a Medication Guide must be provided directly to the patient.
It is sound, provided the pharmacy telephones the patient to summarise the Guide.
It is sound only where the collecting person is not a family member.
It is unsound, because the Guide goes to the patient or the patient's agent at the time of dispensing.
It is unsound, because the Guide must be posted to the patient within 24 hours of dispensing.

explanation.core_reasoning: 21 CFR 208.24(e) requires each authorized dispenser of a product for which a Medication Guide is required to provide a Medication Guide directly to each patient, or to the patient's agent, when the product is dispensed to a patient or to a patient's agent, unless an exemption applies under 208.26. Delivery to an agent is expressly contemplated, so holding the Guide back until the patient appears defers a duty that has already fallen due.

choice_analysis.B: A telephone summary is not the provision of a Medication Guide.
choice_analysis.C: The regulation draws no distinction based on the agent's relationship to the patient.
choice_analysis.D: Correct: the Guide goes to the patient or the patient's agent at the time of dispensing.
choice_analysis.E: No such posting deadline appears in Part 208.

explanation.mpje_trap: The pharmacy's reasoning is patient-centred and sounds careful, which disguises that it postpones a duty the regulation attaches to the act of dispensing.

reasoning_steps: Confirm a Medication Guide is required for the product
Identify who is receiving the product on this occasion
Provide the Guide to that person at the time of dispensing

questions.stem: A customer at a Massachusetts pharmacy counter asks to buy 5 grams of pseudoephedrine base today. He mentions that he bought 5 grams elsewhere eleven days ago. Which statements about the federal quantity limits are correct? Select all that apply.

choices.text: A regulated seller may sell him up to 7.5 grams in a single calendar day.
The pharmacy is the party federally restricted to 3.6 grams per purchaser per day.
Today's sale would exceed the 3.6 gram daily seller restriction.
Buying a further 5 grams within the 30-day window would put the purchaser over the 9 gram limit.
The 9 gram limit applies to sellers rather than to purchasers.

explanation.core_reasoning: The two limits bind different parties under different instruments. 21 CFR 1314.20(a) restricts a regulated seller from selling any purchaser more than 3.6 grams of pseudoephedrine base in a single calendar day, so a 5 gram sale is over the seller's daily ceiling. 21 U.S.C. 844(a) makes it unlawful for any person to purchase at retail more than 9 grams during a 30-day period, so a purchaser who already bought 5 grams eleven days ago would cross that prohibition. The 7.5 gram figure in 21 CFR 1314.20(b) is a 30-day limit and applies to mobile retail vendors.

choice_analysis.A: 7.5 grams is a 30-day figure for mobile retail vendors, not a daily allowance.
choice_analysis.B: The daily restriction does bind the seller, but this option omits that the sale here exceeds it.
choice_analysis.C: Correct: 5 grams in one day is above the 3.6 gram daily seller restriction.
choice_analysis.D: Correct: 5 plus 5 grams inside 30 days crosses the 9 gram retail purchase prohibition.
choice_analysis.E: The 9 gram limit is framed as a prohibition on the person purchasing at retail.

related_facts: Massachusetts requirements apply alongside the federal limits rather than instead of them
explanation.mpje_trap: Three real figures are in play and each belongs to a different party or period, so a candidate who remembers the numbers but not who they bind can pick any of them.

reasoning_steps: Separate the seller's daily restriction from the purchaser's 30-day prohibition
Apply the daily figure to today's proposed sale
Add the earlier purchase to test the 30-day purchase prohibition

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist reads a journal piece arguing that a particular Schedule VI medicine is being diverted and should be watched. Her pharmacy does not report its dispensing to the Prescription Monitoring Program. What determines whether that dispensing becomes reportable?

choices.text: The pharmacy's own assessment that the drug carries a bona fide potential for abuse.
Rescheduling of the drug out of Schedule VI into Schedules II through V.
A prescriber's request that the pharmacy report its dispensing of the drug.
A determination by the Commissioner, followed by notification to dispensers.
Publication of the diversion evidence in the professional literature.

explanation.core_reasoning: 105 CMR 700.012(C)(8) provides that the Commissioner may determine that a drug is an additional drug for the purposes of 105 CMR 700.012 because it carries a bona fide potential for abuse, on factors including addiction risk, known recreational use, known regular diversion for misuse, and known contribution to overdose. Upon making such a determination the Commissioner shall notify all dispensers that they must begin to report the dispensing of that additional drug as directed in 105 CMR 700.012(A). The duty arrives with the determination and the notification.

choice_analysis.A: The factors guide the Commissioner's determination; the pharmacy does not make it.
choice_analysis.B: Rescheduling would bring the drug in through 700.012(A)(1), but it is not what the additional-drug route requires.
choice_analysis.C: A prescriber has no role in creating the reporting duty.
choice_analysis.D: Correct: the Commissioner determines, then notifies all dispensers.
choice_analysis.E: Evidence of diversion is one of the factors, not the operative event.

related_facts: Gabapentin is reported under this route rather than by rescheduling
explanation.mpje_trap: The journal evidence tracks the statutory factors closely, which makes it feel like the trigger. The trigger is the Commissioner's act, not the evidence behind it.

reasoning_steps: Identify the drug's current schedule and reporting status
Locate who holds the power to designate an additional drug
Wait for the determination and the notification before treating the duty as live
